segments.text: International institutions are permanent bodies created by states to cooperate, make decisions, administer regimes or settle disputes.
Study legal personality, constituent instruments, membership, organs, powers, privileges and responsibility. The UN is the main example, but regional and specialized organizations also matter.

An international organization is created by states through a constituent instrument that establishes organs, functions and powers. It is not simply a conference or informal coalition. Legal personality allows the organization to hold rights and duties, enter agreements, possess privileges and immunities, and perform functions distinct from those of its member states.
The classic legal question is not whether an organization has the same sovereignty as a state—it ordinarily does not—but what legal capacity is necessary for the functions assigned to it.

Express powers are written into the constituent treaty. Implied powers may be inferred when they are necessary for the organization to perform its assigned functions, subject to the legal limits of the constituent instrument. The doctrine prevents the organization from being ineffective while also guarding against unlimited institutional authority.

Responsibility and accountability follow from institutional autonomy. An organization can incur legal responsibility for conduct attributable to it under the relevant legal framework, while member states may have separate responsibilities of their own.

blocks.text: The United Nations as the core model

segments.text: The UN is the most useful model because its Charter creates principal organs with distinct roles: the General Assembly, Security Council, Economic and Social Council, International Court of Justice, Secretariat and the historically inactive Trusteeship Council. The Security Council has primary responsibility for international peace and security under the Charter, while the General Assembly has broad deliberative and recommendation functions.
Specialized agencies and regional organizations operate under separate constituent instruments. Their powers should be examined from those instruments rather than assumed from the UN model.

items.text: An international organization is created by an agreement or constituent instrument that gives it organs, functions and powers separate from those of any single member state.
Legal personality allows an organization to hold rights and duties, enter agreements or perform functions on the international plane within its legal capacity.
Express powers are written in the constituent instrument; implied powers may be inferred when necessary to perform assigned functions, subject to the organization's legal framework.
Use the UN as the main model:
distinguish the purposes of principal organs, then apply the same method to specialized or regional organizations.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not treat an international organization as a “world government.” Its authority comes from its constituent legal framework and the powers given by member states.
